Neonates of the Bynoe gecko (Heteronotia binoei SM6) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a mean snout to vent length of 2.1 centimeters [Lb = 2.1 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the lecithotrophic stage of the yolk-sac larva. The corresponding wet weight at birth, calculated from the length-mass allometry established for this lineage, is approximately 0.19 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.19 grams], placing newborns among the smaller members of the gekkonid assemblage in arid Australia. Incubation experiments conducted at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C] reveal that the average incubation duration from oviposition to eclosion is 88.9 days [ab = 88.9 days], a developmental period characteristic of temperate-zone geckos and likely an adaptation to the cool, unpredictable thermal regimes of the species' semi-arid habitats. This extended embryogenesis, coupled with the substantial yolk investment required to sustain growth until the chorion ruptures, imposes a clear trade-off between clutch frequency and offspring size that shapes the early life history of this parthenogenetic form.

Upon reaching adulthood, Bynoe geckos attain an ultimate snout to vent length of 5.9 centimeters [Li = 5.9 centimeters], a body size that defines the upper limit of somatic growth in this lineage. From this length, the allometric equation yields an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5.44 grams [Wwi = approximately 5.44 grams], which is comparable to values reported for other small-bodied Heteronotia populations across the Australian interior. The onset of reproductive maturity, based on the smallest gravid female captured during field surveys, occurs at a snout to vent length of 4.8 centimeters [Lp = 4.8 centimeters], although this figure likely underestimates the true population mean due to sampling constraints imposed by the difficulty of detecting early breeding individuals. At this pubertal size, the predicted wet weight is roughly 2.62 grams [Wwp = roughly 2.62 grams], marking the threshold at which a juvenile transitions to a reproductively active adult capable of egg production under favorable environmental conditions.

Reproductive output in this unisexual species is characterized by a moderate maximum rate, with females producing approximately 4.4 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 4.4 offspring per year] when maintained under controlled thermal conditions at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. This annual output is achieved through the production of roughly 2.2 clutches per year, each clutch containing two eggs. The ability to sustain this level of egg production is tightly linked to the thermal environment; lower temperatures reduce both clutch frequency and the rate of follicular development, highlighting the importance of thermoregulatory behavior in determining annual reproductive success. Field observations confirm that gravid individuals actively seek sun-exposed microhabitats to maintain body temperatures near this optimum during the breeding season.

Longevity records for Heteronotia binoei SM6 indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], based on the recapture of an individual marked as an adult by Kearney, Moritz, and Roberts at Paynes Find Station and encountered again 15 years later at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This figure may be an underestimate, as Bauer reports captive specimens living for 13.6 years, and the recapture interval does not account for the individual's age at initial marking. The low ambient temperatures typical of the species' winter dormancy periods, estimated at around 20 °C [T = 20 °C], are thought to contribute to this extended longevity by slowing the accumulation of cellular damage and reducing the metabolic costs associated with sustained activity. Compared to other small gekkonids, which rarely exceed five to eight years in the field, this lifespan is exceptional and likely reflects a slow pace of life coupled with low extrinsic mortality in the stable, resource-poor environments the species occupies.

The timing of first reproduction in this gecko is tightly coupled to the incubation period and subsequent growth trajectory. Under thermal conditions of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the age at first breeding is estimated at approximately 212 days after hatching [tR = approximately 212 days after hatching], a value derived from summing the incubation duration at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] with the post-hatching growth period required to reach pubertal size. This interval places the species on a relatively fast track to reproductive maturation compared to many nocturnal lizards of similar body mass, an advantage that may facilitate rapid population growth in ephemeral habitats. The capacity for sperm storage in this parthenogenetic form is minimal, as all individuals are female and reproduction is clonal, so the timing of vitellogenesis and ovulation is driven entirely by endogenous hormonal cycles rather than by the presence of mates. Post-reproductive senescence has not been systematically documented, but the species appears capable of breeding annually throughout most of its adult lifespan.
